title: My brother invited me to our parents' old diner for one last breakfast. When I arrived, he'd already sold the building — but the new owner refused to give him the money (PART 2)

blocks.text: …I took the menu with shaking hands. I recognized my father's handwriting immediately, and then, at the bottom, my own: a big, wobbly signature in pencil. DONNA, AGE 9.

The agreement was three lines long. "I, Earl Whitaker, give my daughter Donna full ownership of the biscuit recipe she helped her mother invent this summer, forever. Whoever uses it has to pay her. Witnessed by Hazel Whitaker."

I remembered that summer. I was nine. Mama was trying to make her biscuits fluffier, and I dumped a whole carton of buttermilk into the bowl by accident and then, panicking, added an extra spoon of baking powder and a little honey to cover it up. They were the best biscuits she'd ever made. Daddy laughed so hard he wrote me a contract on the back of a menu as a joke.
He'd had it notarized the following week, and a copy filed with the family lawyer.

The buyer, Mr. Hollis, was the chief executive of a Southern grocery chain. In 2003, my brother Steven had licensed "Whitaker's Famous Biscuits" to Mr. Hollis's company, which sold them frozen in four hundred stores. Steven signed the licensing deal claiming he owned the recipe and had collected the royalties ever since: more than two million dollars over twenty-three years. I'd seen the biscuits in the freezer aisle and thought it was sweet that the family name lived on. I never asked where the money went.
When Mr. Hollis's company decided to buy the diner itself, to use as a flagship restaurant, their lawyers did a thorough search of the family records. They found the menu in the old lawyer's files.
Under the agreement, the recipe belonged to me, and so did every royalty payment.
"I'm not finishing a deal with someone who doesn't own what he sold me," Mr. Hollis said. "I'd rather deal with the woman who invented it."

Steven didn't argue. He sat in the booth across from me for a long time, staring at his coffee. Then he said, "I always meant to tell you." I believed he meant it. I also believed he'd have kept not telling me forever.

Our lawyers worked it out. Steven agreed to repay a large part of the royalties over time. The grocery chain signed a new license with me. The diner was never sold. I bought Steven's share of the building with the first royalty check.
Whitaker's is open again. Same red booths, same neon sign. I make the biscuits myself every morning, with an extra spoon of baking powder and a little honey.
The menu is framed on the wall by the register. Customers always ask about the signature at the bottom. I tell them it's the best deal I ever made.
